weakness: The belt-speed measurement from the head camera segmented the belt with absolute gray thresholds (belt darker than 110, motion above 12). Under dimmer, warmer light (35%) the table fell below the dark threshold, the belt top was never found, and the pipeline silently fell back to a nominal speed; the release timing was then off by up to 20% of a 6 s ride and half the blocks missed the moving bowl.
how_found: Listing what the camera code assumes about appearance: every threshold was a raw pixel value tuned on the default render, and lighting is the most common thing that differs between a lab and a deployment.
why_missed: The thresholds were chosen by looking at frames from one lighting condition, and the fallback (nominal speed) hid the perception failure instead of surfacing it; with the nominal speed the task still succeeded often enough to look plausible.
fix: Normalise each frame set by its own bright background (90th-percentile gray mapped to a fixed level) before applying the dark/motion/red thresholds; verified offline on frames at 0.2x, 0.35x and 1.8x light that the speed error stays within 1%.
general_rule: Make every image threshold relative to a reference measured in the same image (e.g. normalise by the background brightness), and treat a perception step that returns nothing as a failure to report or retry rather than silently substituting a nominal value.

weakness: The pipeline never asked for obstacles other than the belt and blocker, and planned every move with the planner's default world (table only). Two static bars over the belt ends (one beside the pick area) made the open fingers catch on a bar during the approach (the gripper then 'held' the bar), and the carried block was swept into a bar. Repairs that queried get_obstacles and cleared the bars by height exposed a second weakness: with the payload carried higher, long or fallback (orientation-free) plans let the arm pick a different joint configuration and swing; once a swing passed the held block low over the belt past the place line, the task's first-contact check failed for the episode.
how_found: Reading which motions pass obstacles to the planner: only the carry did, with a hand-picked list, while the planner models neither the open fingers nor the held object.
why_missed: In the default scene nothing stands near the paths, so every planned move happened to be clear; a planner that returns success was treated as proof that the motion was harmless.
fix: Not recovered within the repair budget (best 0.7 with: obstacles from get_obstacles; transit and carry heights computed so fingertips and payload clear every box in the straight corridor; obstacle-aware orientation-holding plans first, table-only plans only for vertical moves, no free plans while holding; arrival checked after every move; grasp verified by lifting and re-detecting; pick-carry retried on loss). Remaining failures: the right arm's plans at the higher carry height wandered or failed (start inside inflated boxes, joint-configuration flips). Pipeline reverted to the round-1 version; the attempt is in dev/pipeline_v3_attempt.py.
general_rule: Give the motion planner every perceived obstacle on every move and separately clear whatever the planner does not model (open fingers, the held object) by explicit margins; then check after each move that the tool arrived and the payload is still held, and never accept an unconstrained replan while carrying something near a region where contact has consequences.

weakness: Two things broke under bars hung across the belt over the release zone. (1) The release point was one fixed spot (3.5 cm before the place line) and the gripper descended vertically onto it without checking what was above; the arm or the carried block hit the bar. (2) The camera belt-speed estimate measured the belt length as the longest dark run per image row; the bright bars split the run, so pixels-per-metre and the speed came out 10-60% wrong, and the release timing missed the moving bowl. Static occluders next to the matching window also biased the measured pattern shift towards zero (2-5%).
how_found: Questioning 'the release point is free': the pipeline used the edge of the allowed zone nearest the target because it shortens the ride, but never looked at that spot; a bracket or sensor over a conveyor's infeed is common.
why_missed: In the default scene the whole allowed zone was empty, so the first choice always worked; and the vision step was only tested on scenes where nothing lay across the belt.
fix: Release point: scan the allowed zone from the place line back towards the load edge and take the first spot whose vertical column (open-gripper footprint, from the belt up 35 cm) is free of every perceived obstacle; pass all perceived obstacles to the planner for the carry. Vision: join dark runs separated by short gaps before taking the belt's extent, and keep only pixels whose whole shift window is moving. Verified offline on all stored frame sets (default, lighting, camera, bars): speed error within 1%.
general_rule: When the goal allows a region rather than a point, choose the point inside it by checking that the tool's whole approach volume is free, and make image measurements of a surface robust to static things lying across it (bridge gaps, exclude stationary pixels from motion matching) instead of assuming an unobstructed view.

weakness: A guard cover over the middle 22 cm of the conveyor hid part of the belt from the head camera. The speed measurement took the belt's image length from one contiguous dark run per row (gaps up to 25 px joined); the cover cut the run into two pieces, so the length, the pixel scale and the speed were off by 2-4x (estimates of 0.17-0.22 m/s for a 0.06 m/s belt, or no estimate), and the release timing against the moving bowl became a coin flip.
how_found: Questioning C3 (both belt ends visible): after the bar fix the scale still depended on seeing one unbroken belt surface between two edges; guards and covers over conveyors are normal. v9 (14 cm cover) was rejected at 0.6 because a wrong timing still hits the bowl about half the time, so the cover was widened (v10).
why_missed: The round-3 fix only bridged narrow gaps; it still assumed the belt is one object in each row, rather than asking which pixels carry the moving pattern.
fix: Per row and frame, the belt extent is now the span of all dark pieces that carry the moving pattern (pieces without motion, such as an arm or a cover, do not count), then RANSAC over rows and median over frames as before. A second, independent scale (place line to load edge, oriented by the pattern's motion direction) is kept as a fallback when no full extent is found. Offline on every stored frame set (default, light, camera, bars, cover) the speed error is within 1%; eval: base, v1, v5, v10 all 1.0.
general_rule: Make image measurements of a surface robust to static things lying across it (bridge gaps, exclude stationary pixels from motion matching) instead of assuming an unobstructed view.

weakness: Under a strongly red-tinted light (colour [1.0, 0.35, 0.3]) every gray belt pixel passed the 'red' test (R minus max(G, B) > 60 after brightness normalisation), so the whole belt was dropped from the pattern matching, no speed estimate came out, and the pipeline fell back to the nominal belt speed: release timing became a coin flip (s_break 0.5).
how_found: After round 1 normalised brightness, the remaining appearance assumption in the camera code was the colour test for the red place line and blocker, which silently assumes white light.
why_missed: Round 1 fixed the threshold for the symptom it saw (overall brightness) with one global gain instead of asking which reference every image test depends on; colour tests were left on raw channel differences.
fix: Normalise each colour channel separately by its own 90th percentile (white balance against the background) before any gray or colour test. Offline on all stored frame sets the speed error stays within 1%; eval: base 1.0, v1 0.9, v5 0.9 (the two misses were CUDA out-of-memory at reset, the pipeline never ran), v10 1.0, v11 1.0.
general_rule: Make every image threshold relative to a reference measured in the same image (e.g. normalise by the background brightness), and treat a perception step that returns nothing as a failure to report or retry rather than silently substituting a nominal value.
